## After the first seven chapters: can it scale to a district?

My family has a placer claim outside Nome, and sorting out what the
ground under it is actually made of, the single-claim deep dive that
became [bearcub](https://johnsondevco.com/bearcub/bear_cub.html), is
where this whole project started. After building the first seven pieces
of the portfolio, I began to see how they might come together and run
at the scale of a whole mining district rather than one claim. I began
to wonder how far the parts would stretch.

Could the automated pipeline I built for that one claim (Chapter 1) be
pointed at the entire Nome district? Could I marry it to the regional
prospectivity modeling (Chapters 2 and 4) and the validation discipline
that kept those models from fooling me (Chapter 5)? Could goldbug's
public-land-law layer (Chapter 3) extend to Alaska, where ANCSA (the
1971 Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act) reshaped land ownership into
something very different from the federal open-land system in the Lower
48? Could the drill-record machinery reach past Bear Cub to the
district's other holdings? And could all the dark data the project
keeps ingesting (not just the drill logs, but the USGS reports, the
mining-engineer reports, the KARDEX, MAS, and MIN mineral-record sets)
feed a knowledge graph that in turn trains the prospectivity models?

This chapter is where those questions get answered, some with a working
result and some with a candid "not yet." It is the closing synthesis:
the regional models, the drill-record machinery, the land-law tool, and
the dark-data corpus, all turned on one district at once.

## How the earlier chapters answer the questions

Most of the answers already exist in the earlier chapters. Cape Nome is
where they get pointed at one district together, and the rest of this
chapter is what came back.

The single-claim pipeline from Chapter 1 (the archival drill logs, the
three-dimensional gravel-and-bedrock model, the title puzzle) showed
that one claim's worth of dark data can be turned into a model you can
stand on. The regional work in Chapters 2 and 4 is the machinery for
learning where ore sits from public geoscience data. Chapter 5 is the
discipline that decides whether any of those numbers mean anything,
which on this district turns out to be the whole game: one of the two
headline numbers here survives that discipline and one does not.
[goldbug](https://johnsondevco.com/goldbug/) (Chapter 3) is the
land-law layer that turns a probability surface into a map of the
parcels you can legally stake, now extended onto Alaska ground.
Underneath all of it is the dark-data corpus and the knowledge graph
that consolidates it, which is where most of the actual work went and
where the project is headed next.

So this chapter has four things to report: a placer model that survives
the Chapter 5 wringer, a lode model that does not, a knowledge graph
assembled from the district's dark data, and a candid account of what
is working now versus what is still to come.

## Testing the two headline numbers

The [methodology note on the front page](https://johnsondevco.com/ai-minerals/)
covers the traps that turn a high score into a lie: label leak,
restriction of range, and spatial leakage. They are the through-line
of the whole portfolio, so I will not relitigate them here, beyond the
one rule they all reduce to: take the impressive number, build the
test designed to expose it as luck, and report whatever is left
standing.

Two of this chapter's headline numbers went through that wringer. One
survived and one did not, and the one that did not is the more
interesting story.

## The placer model that held up

Start with the good news, because there isn't always good news.

My first map of the district was a knowledge-driven model: I encoded
what Tuck's bulletin says about where the old beach lines run, scored
every cell in the district by how well it matches a known beach stand,
and served that. It was a reasonable picture of the surface beaches.
But when I scored it against the district's known placer occurrences,
the ones recorded in the USGS Alaska Resource Data File, it came in at
`0.444`[^placer-report], which is below a coin flip. It is a faithful map of the coastal beach lines,
and the coastal beach lines are not where most of the recorded placer
gold in this district actually is. A lot of it is up the creeks.

So I built a second model that does not start from my beliefs about
beaches at all. It learns directly from the terrain and surface
geology: elevation, slope, the shape of the land, the drift and
alluvium polygons. The labels are the recorded occurrences; the model
figures out for itself what those places have in common. Under
spatial-block cross-validation, holding out whole regions at a time, it
scored `0.733`[^placer-report]. With a 300-meter buffer around each
held-out block, so the test ground is genuinely separated from the
training ground, it held at `0.741`. That is the one result in this
chapter I would call a deliverable: a terrain-and-geology model that
ranks the district's placer ground well, and keeps ranking it well
once you hold out whole regions of the map and buffer a gap around them
so it cannot read the answer off a nearby training point.

![Placer prospectivity scored against the recorded ARDF placer occurrences in the district. The earlier knowledge-overlay map (left) ranks below chance because it is a beach-line map and most of the recorded gold is up the creeks. The terrain-and-geology model (center, right), now the surface served on goldbug, holds up under spatial-block cross-validation and again under a buffered cross-validation that separates the test ground from the training ground.](data/derived/portfolio_charts/thumbs/ch1_nome_placer_headline_auc.png)

I want to be careful about what that does and does not mean. `0.733`
is a useful ranking, not a treasure map. It says the model concentrates
the known occurrences toward the high-scoring end of the district far
better than chance, after I have done the work to keep it from cheating.
It does not say any particular cell has gold in it. This terrain model
is now the surface served on goldbug: the live tool ranks each patented
claim and each open parcel by it, on one calibrated scale. The
knowledge-overlay map it replaced is the analysis that first told me
the beach-line picture was ranking the wrong thing.

![The knowledge-overlay surface of the district's beach lines, draped over the Cape Nome coast: my first map, and the one that scores below chance against the recorded occurrences because the recorded gold is largely up the creeks. It is a clean picture of the surface beaches; it is also the map the terrain-and-geology model, now served on goldbug, replaced.](data/derived/portfolio_charts/thumbs/ch1_nome_placer.png)

## How the placer model is built

The setup is the standard presence/background frame for mineral
prospectivity, which is worth stating plainly because whether the
result means anything turns on it.

**Labels.** The positives are the `65` placer occurrences inside the
Cape Nome area of interest that the ARDF records as real, pulled from a
knowledge graph that consolidates ARDF and several other sources (more
on that below). The negatives are a background sample of `2,000` cells
drawn from across the district. This is "presence/background," not
"presence/absence": the background is not known-barren ground, it is
just the district at large, and the model learns what distinguishes the
occurrence sites from the district average.

**Covariates.** The inputs are terrain and geology, all from public
data: the IfSAR digital elevation model (a `5`-meter radar elevation
surface for Alaska), slope and a topographic-position index derived
from it, distance to mapped faults, an aeromagnetic layer, and the
surface-geology unit at each cell. No gold geochemistry in this model,
on purpose; the geochemistry is where the next lie hides, and I deal
with it in the lode section.

**The test.** Spatial-block cross-validation: the district is cut into
blocks, whole blocks are held out, the model trains on the rest and is
scored on the held-out occurrences, and the scores are pooled across
folds. Then the same thing again with a `300`-meter buffer carved
around each held-out block so no test point sits next to a training
point. The buffered score sitting slightly above the unbuffered one
(`0.741` against `0.733`) is the reassuring direction: it means the
result is not an artifact of points leaking across the fold boundary.
The full protocol and the covariate construction are in the appendix.

## The lode model that did not

Here is the one I had to talk myself out of.

Placer gold comes from somewhere. It weathers out of gold-bearing
quartz veins in the bedrock, the lodes, and washes downstream to
collect in the gravels. So a natural next step is to model the lodes
directly: where are the hard-rock sources? I built a structural model,
terrain and geology and faults and aeromagnetics, on the known lode
occurrences, and at first it looked good. On my initial test area it
scored about `0.80`[^lode-report], and I was fairly pleased with it.

But before believing a number you have to check that the labels are
not quietly encoding the answer, and these were. My test area was a
small box around the placer core, and inside that box every known lode
sat up in the schist hills while almost everything I had drawn as
background sat down on the flat coastal plain. The model was not
learning what a gold lode looks like. It was learning to tell a hill
from a beach. That is restriction of range, exactly the second lie, and
it is seductive because the number is real; the model genuinely
separates the two classes. It just separates them on elevation, not on
geology.

So I redrew the test across the whole district, out to the Solomon
quad, pulling in the Big Hurrah lode and the other hinterland sources,
so the background ground is now also upland. The score fell to
`0.62`, and to `0.58` under the buffered spatial cross-validation[^lode-dist-report].
That is barely better than a coin flip. The structural signal that
looked strong in the small box does not survive being asked to work
across the real district.

![The lode mirage. In a small box around the placer core (left), the structural model scores about 0.80, because the lodes are in the hills and the background is on the coast. Across the whole district (right), where the background is also upland, the same model falls to roughly chance. The geochemistry reads higher but the elements it uses trail gold by definition, so that number is circular.](data/derived/portfolio_charts/thumbs/ch1_nome_lode_mirage.png)

There is a tempting escape hatch, and it is the third lie. If I add
stream-sediment geochemistry, arsenic, antimony, bismuth, mercury,
tungsten, the pathfinder elements, the lode model jumps back up to
about `0.805`[^lode-dist-report]. But those pathfinders are precisely
the elements that travel with gold; using them to predict gold is
close to using gold to predict gold. The number is high and it means
almost nothing.

So the lode result is a negative result. I do not have a validated,
independent lode-prospectivity signal for this district that survives
a test built to break it, and I am reporting that rather than shipping the
`0.80` and hoping nobody redraws the box. A negative result that you
caught yourself is worth more than a positive one you didn't.

## Dark data, turned into structured evidence

This is the part the prospectivity numbers sit on top of, and the part
with the most room left to run. A mining district throws off a century
of paper: drill logs, USGS bulletins, mining-engineer reports, state
mineral-record cards, court and probate files, leases and conveyances.
Almost none of it is in a form a model can read. Turning that dark data
into structured evidence, records with coordinates, identities, and a
source you can click back to, is a data-integration problem before it
is a modeling problem, and it is where a lot of the actual work went.

The occurrences and the historical record come from several public
corpora that do not agree with each other: the USGS ARDF, the MRDS
mineral-resource database, the Cobb 1978 occurrence compilation for the
Nome quad, and the Alaska KARDEX, several hundred typewriter-era state
mineral-record cards that exist only as scanned images. Pulling these
together means reconciling deposit names, coordinate systems, and
production qualifiers, then resolving the duplicates so that the KARDEX
card, the ARDF entry, the Cobb record, and the drill log for the same
piece of ground all collapse to one identity. That consolidation lives
in a sibling knowledge-graph project and feeds this model its labels;
switching the placer labels to the graph's datum-corrected occurrences
left the AUCs identical to three decimal places, which is the check
that the switch changed the plumbing and not the answer.

The same graph is what lets the family chain-of-title puzzle resolve:
the KARDEX cards and the recorded documents name the operators and
conveyances, and the graph links them back to the claim. You can open
it three ways and poke at it yourself: a tabular SQL browser, a spatial
map of claims and occurrences, and a linked per-entity wiki where each
claim, document, and operator has its own page. On the goldbug side,
the claim detail pages now carry the attached graph records, so
clicking a survey shows you the documents behind it. The point of that
per-claim source trail is that every label the model trains on, and
every parcel goldbug ranks, can be traced back to the scanned card or
report it came from.

Where this is headed is a loop: fold more of the dark-data corpus into
the graph, and let the graph feed the prospectivity models better
labels and richer covariates than the public occurrence files alone
can. The KARDEX, MAS, and MIN mineral-record sets, the USGS and
mining-engineer reports, and the drill logs the district generated over
a century are each a corpus the model has not seen yet. Closing that
loop, the graph feeding the models and not just the model reading the
graph, is the goal; right now the graph supplies the labels and the
source trail, and the richer covariate feed is still ahead.

## What's working now, and what's still to come

It is worth being plain about the gap between where this stands and
where it is going.

**Working now.** The placer model that survives a test built to break
it exists and is the surface goldbug serves: the live tool ranks each
patented claim and each open parcel on one calibrated scale. The lode
model is a negative result I trust precisely because I tried to make it
fail and it did. The knowledge graph is built from the ARDF, MRDS,
Cobb, and KARDEX corpora, and you can open it through the three viewers
and follow any claim back to its source documents. goldbug is live, and
the terrain placer model is the surface it serves.

**Still to come.** The richer dark-data corpora are not yet folded in.
The Cape Nome recorded documents, the locations and assessment work and
leases and conveyances the district generated over a century, are
public and largely un-digitized. The Janin 1912 drill logs for the Bear
Cub holdings were rescued from an archive at the Huntington. And the
largest landowner in the district, the Alaska Gold Company, a Bering
Straits Native Corporation subsidiary, holds on the order of ten
thousand drill logs we are pursuing access to through a collaboration.
Each of those is a dark-data corpus the model has never seen. The MAS
and MIN record sets are still being ingested, and the
knowledge-graph-into-model-training loop is a goal, not yet a working
result. The lode question is open too: I do not have an independent
lode signal that survives the district-scale test, and finding one
would need dispersed, peninsula-wide labels I do not have yet.

I would rather name the trajectory and tell you exactly where on it we
are than dress up the demo as the destination.

## Appendix: the numbers and the protocol {#appendix}

<details>
<summary>Full metrics, cross-validation protocol, and what each number is</summary>

All figures below are read directly from the committed evaluation
reports under `data/derived/nome_placer/`; the figures in the chapter
are rendered from the same JSON, so every number on a chart is the live
computed value.

**Placer presence/background** (`mpm_onshore_presence_cv.py`, `65`
occurrences vs `2,000` background):

| Model | AUC | Note |
|---|---:|---|
| v3.1 knowledge-overlay composite (first map, since replaced) | 0.444 | below chance; a beach-line map mis-ranks the upland creek placers |
| Terrain + geomorphology, spatial-block CV (now the live map) | 0.733 | the regional result that survives spatial CV |
| Terrain + geomorphology, buffered 300 m | 0.741 | buffered ≥ unbuffered, so no across-fold leak |
| Full model incl. Au geochemistry, spatial-block CV | 0.686 | near-circular; geochem Au is a gold detector, excluded from the headline |

**Lode, small box vs district** (`mpm_lode_presence_cv.py`,
`mpm_lode_district_cv.py`):

| Scope | Model | AUC |
|---|---|---:|
| Small box (30 lodes, placer core) | structural/terrain, spatial CV | 0.802 |
| Small box | structural/terrain, buffered 300 m | 0.791 |
| District (93 lodes, incl. Big Hurrah) | structural/terrain, spatial CV | 0.620 |
| District | structural/terrain, buffered 300 m | 0.582 |
| District | full incl. stream-sed geochem | 0.805 (circular) |
| District | pathfinders only (As Sb Bi Hg W) | 0.691 (circular) |

**Cross-validation protocol.** Spatial-block CV cuts the district into
blocks on the projected grid (EPSG:3338), holds out whole blocks, trains
on the remainder, and pools the out-of-fold predictions before scoring a
single AUC. The buffered variant additionally drops any training cell
within `300` m of a held-out block, so a test point cannot be scored by
a training neighbor. Note: the harness reports one pooled out-of-fold
AUC per model, not a per-fold distribution, so the chapter figures show
point estimates without fold error bars; persisting per-fold AUCs for an
error-bar version is a small follow-up.

**The restriction-of-range diagnosis.** The small-box lode result
(`0.802`) is an artifact of the box geometry: every lode is upland
schist, the background is coastal-flat, and the model's top features are
elevation, distance-to-fault, and slope. Widening to the district
(adding the Big Hurrah lode and the Solomon-quad hinterland, so the
background is also upland) collapses it to `0.620` / `0.582`. The
structural law does not transfer.

**Why geochemistry is excluded from the headline.** The stream-sediment
pathfinder suite (arsenic, antimony, bismuth, mercury, tungsten) trails
gold mineralization by definition, so a model using it to predict gold
occurrences is close to circular. It is reported here for completeness
and kept out of both headline numbers.

**Determinism.** The cross-validation harness is pinned (`n_jobs=1`,
positives lexsorted before the spatial-block split) to remove
cross-process random-forest jitter of roughly `0.02` AUC; the reported
numbers are reproducible run to run.

</details>

[^placer-report]: `data/derived/nome_placer/mpm_onshore/mpm_onshore_presence_report.json`, produced by `scripts/nome_placer/mpm_onshore_presence_cv.py`.

[^lode-report]: `data/derived/nome_placer/mpm_lode/mpm_lode_presence_report.json` (small-box test, 30 lodes), produced by `scripts/nome_placer/mpm_lode_presence_cv.py`.

[^lode-dist-report]: `data/derived/nome_placer/mpm_lode/mpm_lode_district_report.json` (district-wide, 93 lodes incl. Big Hurrah), produced by `scripts/nome_placer/mpm_lode_district_cv.py`.
